articleTitle: International Conference on Rural Telecommunications (Conf. Publ. No.286)
A nonhierarchical rural network with decentralized control
abstract: Describes the design of the Delft Rural Telephone System (DRTS). This system was designed with special attention to its future use in rural areas in developing countries. The main characteristics of the system are the use of digital techniques (in both switching and transmission). The nonhierarchical networks structure, the application of modular switching nodes and special features for remote and/or computer assisted maintenance. The choice of digital techniques with PCM-TDM will be explained and justified with a look to the future. The advantages of a non-hierarchical network will be explained considering the special needs of developing countries with respect to expandability and reliability. The switching nodes that are used in the design are microprocessor controlled and can be configured in different ways depending on their functions. These functions are transit switching, drop-insert, and subscriber interfacing. Each configuration can be assembled using a limited amount of modular building blocks. These are constructed with modern off-the-shelf telecommunications integrated circuits.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Low cost digital satellite communications for rural areas
abstract: World-wide communications using the UoSAT-2 Digital Communications Experiment have demonstrated the practicality and application of store-and-forward techniques using low Earth orbiting satellites in support of communications in rural areas. These experiments have been made possible primarily by recent developments in VLSI processors and semiconductor mass memory devices. Cost-effective spacecraft engineering techniques pioneered by the University of Surrey have been applied to highly reliable, low-cost satellites produced within short timescales. A pilot experiment, in conjunction with the Amateur Satellite Service, provides routine store-and-forward communications to numerous stations worldwide using the UoSAT-2 DCE. Applying this practical, in-orbit experience, engineers with AMSAT and UoSAT are planning a 'PACSAT' store-and-forward communications payload for the UoSAT-C satellite.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A solution to rural communication problems
abstract: The authors described the telecom scene in rural India and the approach taken by the centre for development of telematics (C-DOT), to modernise it. The C-DOT has come forward with a rural network consisting of rural automatic exchange (RAX), transit RAX (TRAX) and maintenance administration billing system (MABS). The RAX and TRAX employ digital switching. They are designing to function in adverse tropical climates without any special care-for example air conditioning. Though the rural network suits rural India, it applies equally well for the other developing countries. Initially, it aims at providing the basic minimum facilities for rural growth coupled with optimum resource utilisation. A case study of C-DOT RAX at Kittur, a village in Karnataka State, India, is presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of TDX-1A/RSS system to Korean rural network for widening the service area
abstract: The authors consider rural network components, including a discussion of requirements, and give a description of the TDX-1A/RSS system, a digital time division switching system. The network application is discussed, and the model network, including network configuration and economical comparison of alternatives, is described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The Australian digital radio concentrator system-DRCS
abstract: The authors describe the Australian digital radio concentrator system, giving a general description, system range, system components, and multiplexing is discussed, and system supervision is considered. The scope of the civil/structural engineering work is discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrated rural network architecture-the way to go in rural telecommunications
abstract: The authors discuss the objectives of using the most appropriate and differentiated technology in each part of an extended rural network according to optimum engineering, and of providing integrated operation and maintenance for the whole. This objective can be met if all subsystems are designed to use standard type protocols to communicate operation and supervision information. The economic benefits of this system are considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rural telecommunication system in Indonesia
abstract: The particular problems for telecommunications in Indonesia are outlined, and the use of digital technology for rural telecommunications is considered. The requirements for a rural system for Indonesia are given, and the adaptation of the existing system to meet these requirements is discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: UXDS: a digital telephone exchange for world-wide rural networks
abstract: The authors give the background and a system description of the UXDS digital telephone exchange, and consider direct connection to 30-channel PCM. They also discuss aspects of the services and supports needed for rural telecommunications projects.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Analysis of rural subscriber service system, using multiplex radio relay links
abstract: The authors give the basic considerations of a rural communication network, and list the particular requirements of Nepal. Several systems are compared in terms of economy, operation and maintenance, and expandability. An example of an actual system designed for Nepal is given.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A new high capacity TDMA radio system
abstract: The authors consider the problems of providing telephone and data services in rural areas of Canada. A high capacity TDMA system, the SR500, is described, including system dimensions and performance, and common channel signalling is discussed. The importance of the subscriber radio product being able to provide ISDN services is considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rural optical fibre experience in Australia
abstract: The special needs of the Australian rural community in terms of the inter-capital single mode optical fibre installation program are discussed. The author considers the reasons for the choice of 2, 8, and 34 Mbit/s equipment, and describes the construction and installation of the system. Experience, gained from this installation is outlined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fibre optics in developing countries-obstacles and opportunities for rural communities
abstract: Fibre optic systems are increasingly found in almost every sector of the telecommunications networks of developed countries. But what relevance do these developments have to rural communities in developing countries? The authors attempt to answer this question by first reviewing some of the main fibre optic trends in developed countries. This is followed by a brief look at the competing technologies for telecommunications in rural areas of developing countries where fibre is just one among many possible options. They then address some of the main obstacles and opportunities related to applying fibre in rural environments. Finally answers will be given to the question: to what extent is fibre optics an 'appropriate' technology. That is, how does it measure up to the actual needs of developing countries?.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rural optical communications at 2, 8 and 34 Mbit/s
abstract: The special needs of Australian rural communications are discussed, and a high performance single-mode 1300 nm optical system operating at 2, 8, and 34 Mbits/s is described. Design features are described in detail, and the design factors considered by Alcatel Australia in the system development are described. These include operational, environmental, and performance requirements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A satellite DAMA system for rural communications
abstract: Presents and discusses a centralized DAMA system which combines a simple and reliable signalling protocol with quite short access times and very few resources wasted for signalling purposes. The performance analysis of this DAMA system carried out through the results coming from a simulation code, will shown on one hand, that the stations number does not affect too strongly the overall system characteristics in terms of access time when the total amount of signalling traffic is lower than a specified value; on the other, that this access system allows the greatest flexibility of the signalling network ranging from a completely random access to a fully disciplined TDMA (time division multiple access). The telecommunication system described only refers to the telephone traffic management, even though it could easily be applied to other kinds of services as well.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Cost-effective method of data distribution in rural areas using existing satellite video system
abstract: Demonstrates how existing satellite television channels can be used to transmit data without degrading the video or audio signals. In this way, information can be distributed over a wide geographical area to provide an additional, economic service. Although applicable to any type of satellite-transmitted video channel, examples will be given of the proposed data distribution system using Ku-band satellites of the 'medium-power' type, such as the EUTELSAT series. These are geostationary satellites which will not require tracking antennas on earth stations, as the cost of the earth station will be an important consideration in any wide-area rural system. The type of data-disintegration system proposed is essentially a 'point-to-multipoint' transmission, using the satellite as a point source. All that is required of the satellite is that the transponder carrying the video signal should have a footprint covering the geographical area under consideration. In the two examples given, Great Britain is used to demonstrate a typical small country-wide applications, whereas Canada has a large area.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rural telecommunications in a third world country
abstract: This paper looks at the problems encountered in a typical West African country and concludes that the UN intention of ensuring that everyone on the globe is within easy access of a telephone will be very difficult if not most improbable to achieve. The main aim of the paper is to bring the reader 'down to earth' by outlining the very real day-to-day problems faced by telecommunication administrations of emerging nations. British Teleconsult is part of British Telecom Overseas Division and provides consultancy services to foreign administrations. This paper looks at one particular country, Sierra Leone, where operational experience has been built up over at least 5 years.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rural telecommunications in Botswana
abstract: The Botswana Telecommunications Corp., (BTC) has set as its task to provide an automatic telephone service to as many villages as possible with a population in excess of 500. A selection of the technologies used to meet the comparatively small capacity of transmission and switching requirements of the BTC is discussed. These include radio transmission systems, multi-access radio systems, point to point digital radio systems, point to point analogue radio systems, HF radio systems, line transmission systems, open-wire trunk carrier, open-wire subscriber carrier, and cable systems. Several other technologies have been examined and a brief synopsis of these is included.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modernization of the rural network in Sweden
abstract: In the modernisation strategy the network will continue to include the following hierarchical levels: tertiary areas, secondary areas, trunk exchange areas and local exchange areas. The introduction of digital telephone exchanges in rural areas require an AXE parent exchange with characteristics slightly different from those of present applications. It must for instance be possible to modernise existing telephone exchanges without major extensions to the building. Consequently, there are plans for a combination of selected AXE products, intended to provide a specific application for small exchanges.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Appropriate telecommunication technology for rural Africa
abstract: The author outlines the problems of rural telecommunications in Africa, and describes the regional African satellite communication system for the development of Africa (RASCOM). The origin and goals of this project are explained, and the project activities are described. Satellite communication technology as an option for rural communications is discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Family of switching systems for cost effective rural telecommunication services
abstract: The authors describe ESAX ESAX 200, ILT-512, ILT-2048, and MILT-64, for each of these switching systems, system description, system software, and features and facilities are given in the context of cost effective rural telecommunication.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Building block design of large capacity PCM-TDMA subscriber system and direct digital interface to digital exchange
abstract: The authors describe a fully digitised TDMA system, with 64 kbits/s PCM for voice coding/decoding, that can be directly interfaced to a digital exchange. The direct digital interface is described, and the processing and format of the digital signal for the interface discussed. The design of a large capacity PCM-TDMA subscriber radio system is considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A point-to-multipoint digital radio system for rural subscriber areas
abstract: The author considers the criteria that must be taken into account when designing a point-to-multipoint digital radio, giving geographic and environmental conditions. energy resources, personnel, and economic background as the most important. He presents the conceptual aspects which have been followed in the design of the multiple-access digital radio system RURTEL DRRS 2501.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optical cables for rural communication systems
abstract: The authors consider the use of optical cables in rural communications, giving product requirements. The advantages of an optical cable solution are given, and several cable designs are discussed and illustrated. Two possible network designs are shown.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Planning the Irish rural network
abstract: The local network is planned in two stages; a main cable stage, between the exchange, or remote subscriber unit (RSU) and the cross connection point (CCP), and a distribution stage between the CCP and the customer termination (or between exchange and customer termination if no CCP is used). Network treatment and pair gain devices are being evaluated on a continuous basis. Most of the units described here are in use in the network. There are three categories of special device; line treatment gadgets, pair-gain systems and radio systems. The units are described briefly. Devices which were evaluated, but are not in use are included. Ways of serving communities of varying size and location are then discussed. Some cost comparisons are made. The direction of current work on the rural network is indicated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optical access networks in rural telecommunications
abstract: Reviews the basics of optical fibre multiplexing and fibre termination techniques and suggested a number of alternative architectures which could be deployed in rural networks. Two basic multiplexing techniques are time-division multiplexing (TDM) and wavelength division multiplexing (WDM). It is possible to connect many fibres together optically. These joint are highly directional in nature. In order to describe how these types of joint can handle TDM and WDM signals the description is separated into splitters and combiners.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Trends and potential for the use of satellites for rural telecommunications in developing countries
abstract: Identifies those technological trends which have the potential of giving the satellite solution a substantial economic advantage over the terrestrial one. Significant advances have already been achieved in very small aperture terminal (VSAT) technology for burst mode TDM-TDMA transmission for low density data (64 kbps or less). Progressive reductions in voice encoded data rate from 64 kbps to 32, 16 and eventually to 9.6 kbps could help bring VSATs into the rural telecommunications market. Further, improvements in spectrum usage efficiency from TDMA or from more advanced modulation techniques like spread spectrum, combined with higher EIRP transponders, could significantly reduce both the cost of earth stations and space segment tariffs to the point where the economics of rural telephony and low-speed data services become attractive. However, it is important to consider exactly what impact such changes in satellite communication facilities could have, based on as assessment of the total requirements of local networks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rural telecommunications development policy in developing countries
abstract: The author discusses the imbalance between urban and rural telecommunication services, and considers the need for deliberate policy action by all governments concerned. Sources of finance are outlined, and rural telecommunication technology discussed. The importance of standardisation is explained.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rural telecommunications using ARABSAT
abstract: Examines the possibility of providing service to certain remote areas of the United Arab Emirates by satellite links. The communication requirements are: point to point links (4*2 Mb/s) from Das and Delma islands to main land for parenting remote stored program controlled (SPC) exchanges and a subscriber distribution system (SDS) to serve about 120 subscribers in other sparsely populated areas. A satellite based network may be expected to provide an elegant cost effective solution. A digital network using an ARABSAT transponder has, therefore, been designed to investigate this possibility. Since the ground terminals must be located in remote areas a reliable, unattended operation is desirable. Small, nontracking antennas are, therefore, a preferred choice. Power efficient modulation schemes, coding and capacity enhancement techniques have been considered to achieve the most cost effective utilization of resources. Results indicate that the remote earth stations for the point to point links may use antenna sizes in the range of 4.5 m to 7.5 m while those for the SDS links may employ 2.2 m to 4.5 m antennas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A village radio telecommunications system in Sierra Leone
abstract: The networks envisaged would consist of a number of village stations within range of a base station. Each station would consist of a transceiver powered by a solar panel with a lead acid battery to act as a reservoir. The antennae would be simple omnidirectional antennae. The stations are controlled by microprocessor based control units performing the functions of selectively calling other stations, controlling, monitoring and logging battery charging, maintaining a log of station use, measuring output power, VSWR, and signal strengths and of transmitting this information to another station, normally the base. This facilitates remote fault diagnosis and detection of operator misuse, as well as enabling statistics on the use of the network for future planning.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modern telecommunications for rural Alaska
abstract: Discusses the objectives of a rural telephone service, cost, implementation , and social and economic impact. The availability of satellite communications changed the feasibility of providing adequate and reliable service to small villages. The earth station design procured for the original installation allowed the station to grown to eight SCPC voice grade channels and TV receive only services. With its oil revenues during the 1970s, Alaska was able to build an infrastructure using a mix of satellite technology, terrestrial radio links and small digital exchanges.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rural automation-the Kenya experience
abstract: Kenya Posts and Telecommunications Corporation (KP&TC) has embarked on the Rural Automation Programme to improve rural telephone services. This paper outlines some of the user expectations, requirements and limitations when implementing such a programme. The Kenyan situation is treated as a case study where the following issues are discussed: typical characteristics of the Kenyan telecommunications network as it existed prior to rural automation; aims and objectives of the Rural Automation Programme; factors considered when making choices on the equipment, technology and network configuration to be adopted (switching and transmission equipment, building services, power requirements and air conditioning); planning and implementation of the programme; technical personnel development; maintenance philosophy; problems encountered; impact of the Rural Automation Programme on the existing network, on development and on revenues; and future plans.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Planning and modernisation of rural telecommunications services-which technology and why?
abstract: Telecom Australia has a range of options available to provide telecommunication services to customers in rural and remote areas by adopting transmission oriented solutions in combination with the replacement or extension of existing crossbar switching equipment using the AXE-104 and remote multiplexing units. A brief summary is given of a number of possible configurations. The AXE-104 offers flexibility in planning as it does not depend on the availability of digital transmission for interworking with existing analogue switches, yet is able to connect to the ISDN.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A rural communications development in the Caribbean
abstract: Considers various planning functions pertinent to a rural telecommunications system. The digital switching network installed on the Caribbean island of Dominica is outlined and details are given of the development and provision of rural communications on the east coast of the island, using point-to-multipoint microwave radio.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Need for cost effective rural communication services
abstract: The author describes the characteristics of a rural environment, and discusses the telecommunication services that are of relevance in a developing country emphasising the rural requirement. Special points to be noted when planning rural telecommunication services are given, and features of rural switching and transmission equipment are discussed. Economic considerations and maintenance philosophy are also presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Flexible rural systems (telecommunications)
abstract: The authors explain the concepts of flexible rural communications, and discuss requirements for a rural system. A system overview of a rural communication system consisting of exchange interface equipment, local access module, optical and microwave transmission systems, and a network management system is given. System equipment is discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
